content:
Context: Ghost: Mark me.
Hamlet: I will.

Ophelia: Ay, my lord.
Ophelia: I think nothing, my lord.
Ophelia: What is, my lord?
Ophelia: You are merry, my lord.
Hamlet: Who, I?

Ghost: Mark me.
Ghost: My hour is almost come When I to sulf'rous and tormenting flames Must render up myself.
Hamlet: Alas, poor ghost!

Who are you? Who am I?

As Hamlet speaks with his ghostly guide Ophelia, he reflects on his mortality and reflects that he is the last living member of his family line, which has been passed down through generations. He also questions whether it's really him who is haunting him and whether he is truly dead, or if this is merely a hallucination. As for himself, Hamlet acknowledges that he may have been born into wealth and privilege, but he has failed to fulfill his duty towards his family, society, and the world as a whole. The "ghost" is a symbolic representation of his internal struggle, as he grapples with his own identity and purpose amidst death and decay. Ultimately, he realizes that his life was not worth living and that his time has come. Throughout the conversation, Hamnet uses various literary devices such as repetition, metaphor, and imagery to convey his emotions and thoughts. Overall, Hamlett's monologue showcases his introspective and reflective nature, highlighting his complexities as both a person and a character.
